messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The first time David Tran saw his own reflection fracture across the parking garage security camera, he was still gripping the steering wheel of his sedan, his breath caught in his throat. It had happened months ago, during a late shift at St. Jude’s Medical Center, when a stranger stepped from behind a concrete support column and pressed a crumpled knife against David’s left ribs. The cold bite of the blade had driven the air from his lungs, and as he was shoved backward, the exact pressure and tearing sensation in his side had felt unmistakably like the event itself replaying in real time. When the assailant finally tossed his wallet into a storm drain and vanished into the dark, David had run, but the memory did not fade; it settled behind his eyes like a stack of undeveloped photographs he could never look away from. The suddenness of the attack, combined with the weapon’s precise placement against his flank, explained why any rustle in a darkened hallway now triggered a jolt of panic, and why his body still remembered the exact coordinates of the pain. David’s conviction that he was intrinsically flawed for the attack fundamentally reshaped his daily reality. Because he had come to believe his own hesitation had invited the violence, he adopted rigid safety behaviors, constantly checking behind himself at every hospital corridor and scanning patient rooms for concealed figures before entering. Because he viewed himself as fundamentally compromised, his nervous system remained locked in high alert, and the resulting anxiety quickly shattered his sleep, leaving him rigid and exhausted by dawn. Because he viewed himself as fundamentally compromised, his mind refused to contextualize the past, allowing the visual memories of the struggle to surface unfiltered. This chronic sense of threat directly fueled his avoidance behaviors; he began choosing his breakroom seat strictly for its clear lines of sight and rear access, always prioritizing how protected he felt from sudden entry. The constant hyperarousal also sharpened his sensory processing, which in turn made the photographic memories of the garage surface with greater frequency, each flash bringing the phantom ache of the knife against his ribs. The relentless recurrence of these painful visual fragments then cemented his despair, convincing him that nothing good could ever happen to him again, while the emotional drain of his sleeplessness only deepened his belief that he was fundamentally broken. His compulsive mirror checking in the scrub bays and environmental scanning exhausted his cognitive reserves, reinforcing the hopelessness that nothing good could ever happen to him again. As he poured his cognitive resources into these safety behaviors, his mind began to rely on them to keep the intrusions at bay, frantically occupying itself with charting protocols to block the incoming images. However, the hyper-vigilant scanning paradoxically heightened his sensory awareness, which in turn made the memories surface with sharper clarity, creating a tightening loop that consumed his evenings and strained his marriage; David and his wife stopped dining out because he would spend the entire meal tracking the kitchen staff and scanning the windows. What finally brought David Tran to the clinic was a morning when he froze in the medication dispensary, terrified that the quiet hum of the shelves was a prelude to another ambush, and what he hoped for now was simply a way to stop waiting for the next attack.
